message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.31","text":"And in response I said, “Then those who do wrong are not responsible, since it is by God’s judgment that they wrong the righteous.” Peter said, “They most certainly do sin, for they have given themselves over to sinning. Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish justly those who have come to regret their former sins, so that, for the righteous, through punishment of this kind, the evil deeds done before their reorientation may be forgiven, while the ungodly punishers, who desire to maltreat others and are unwilling to reorient, have been permitted to maltreat the righteous in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty. For without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap; in the same way, even the hairs of the righteous are numbered by God.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὅθεν εἰδὼς ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐκλέγεται τιμωρεῖν","chosen":"Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish","rationale":"The subject is understood contextually as God, while the people chosen from among the wrongdoers are the understood subjects of the infinitive “to punish.”"},{"source_quote":"τοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς προτέροις ἁμαρτήμασιν μεταμεληθέντας δικαίως","chosen":"those who have come to regret their former sins ... justly","rationale":"μεταμέλομαι is distinguished from the subsequent μετάνοια language and rendered as regret. δικαίως is attached to the justice of the punishment; it could instead describe their regretting as rightly done."},{"source_quote":"πρὸ τῆς μετανοίας","chosen":"before their reorientation","rationale":"The rendering follows the supplied terminology policy for μετάνοια while not adding an unstated destination such as “toward God.”"},{"source_quote":"μετανοεῖν μὴ θέλουσιν","chosen":"are unwilling to reorient","rationale":"The moral redirection sense of μετανοεῖν is retained without an invented intensifier or destination."},{"source_quote":"εἰς ἀναπλήρωσιν ἰδίας κολάσεως","chosen":"in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty","rationale":"ἀναπλήρωσις denotes filling up or completing, while κόλασις here is the punishment accruing to the ungodly agents."},{"source_quote":"ἄνευ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ βουλῆς οὐδὲ στρουθὸς ἐν παγίδι ἐνπεσεῖν ἔχει","chosen":"without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap","rationale":"βουλή is “counsel” or “purpose,” and the ἔχει plus infinitive construction is represented idiomatically by “can.” The explicitly named trap is retained."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.32","text":"The righteous person is the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature. For example, everyone has it by nature to love those who love them, but the righteous person tries also to love enemies, to bless those who revile him, and, moreover, to pray for enemies. He has mercy on those who wrong him; therefore he also refrains from wronging them in return. Likewise, he blesses those who curse him, gives way to those who strike him, withdraws before those who pursue him, greets those who do not greet him, shares what he has with those who have nothing, wins over the angry person, reconciles the enemy, exhorts the disobedient person, instructs the unbeliever, comforts the mourner, endures when abused, and does not become indignant when treated ungratefully. Having committed himself to loving his neighbor as himself, he has not feared poverty; rather, by distributing his own possessions to those who have nothing, he becomes poor. Nor, indeed, does he punish someone who sins. For the one who loves his neighbor as himself knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished; in the same way, he does not punish those who sin. And just as he wants to be flattered, blessed, and honored, and to have all his sins forgiven him, he himself does this same thing for his neighbor, because he loves that person as himself. In a word, what he wants for himself he also wants for his neighbor. For this is the law of God and of the prophets; this is the teaching of the truth. All this, then, is perfect love toward every human being and is the male part of humaneness, while showing mercy is its female part. This consists in feeding the hungry, providing drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, receiving a stranger, helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon, and, in short, having mercy on anyone amid misfortunes.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὁ τοῦ εὐλόγου ἕνεκα τῇ φύσει μαχόμενος","chosen":"the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature","rationale":"τὸ εὔλογον denotes what is reasonable or warranted by reason. The author’s image of conflict with nature is retained."},{"source_quote":"φιλοῦντας φιλεῖν ... ἐχθροὺς ἀγαπᾶν","chosen":"to love those who love them ... to love enemies","rationale":"The first expression uses φιλέω reciprocally and the second uses ἀγαπάω. English “love” is used for both, while the distinct Greek roots and the contrast between natural reciprocity and enemy-love are disclosed here."},{"source_quote":"προσαδικεῖσθαι ἀπέχεται","chosen":"refrains from wronging them in return","rationale":"The middle infinitive is understood contextually as retaliatory wrongdoing. A more formally passive reading, “refrains from being wronged further,” is grammatically possible but poorly fits the surrounding acts of nonretaliation."},{"source_quote":"τύπτουσιν συγχωρεῖ","chosen":"gives way to those who strike him","rationale":"συγχωρεῖ can mean either “gives way” or, in later usage, “forgives.” “Gives way” preserves the movement imagery reinforced by the following ὑποχωρεῖ, while “forgives those who strike him” remains a viable alternative."},{"source_quote":"ὡς αὐτὸς ἁμαρτήσας οἶδεν τιμωρηθῆναι μὴ θέλειν","chosen":"knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished","rationale":"The aorist participle is read conditionally. It could instead be read as referring to his actual past sin: “knows that, having himself sinned, he does not want to be punished.”"},{"source_quote":"κολακεύεσθαι","chosen":"to be flattered","rationale":"The potentially uncomfortable force of κολακεύω is preserved rather than softened to “treated kindly.”"},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἄρρεν μέρος ... τὸ θῆλυ μέρος","chosen":"the male part ... its female part","rationale":"The author’s gendered division of perfect love and mercy is preserved without harmonization or explanation in the translation text."},{"source_quote":"φιλανθρωπίας","chosen":"humaneness","rationale":"φιλανθρωπία denotes benevolence or love toward humanity; “humaneness” is used consistently here and in the following passage."},{"source_quote":"τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν","chosen":"helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon","rationale":"The rendering formally represents the printed middle/passive participle ἐπιραινόμενον, but its intended subject, attachment, and contextual meaning cannot be securely determined."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν","issue":"The image-checked reading ἐπιραινόμενον ordinarily means “being sprinkled upon” or, in a middle sense, “sprinkling oneself upon.” Its accusative form does not agree with τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ, and neither its attachment nor a contextually coherent contribution to the duty of assisting a prisoner is recoverable with confidence. The translation preserves its formal sense rather than silently replacing it, but no defensible contextual interpretation can presently be established.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"12.33","text":"After hearing this, I said, “These things can be done, but I do not think that the ability to benefit enemies while enduring every outrage from them can belong to human nature.” Peter answered, “You have spoken correctly. For humaneness, since it is a cause of immortality, is given at great cost.” And I said, “How, then, can it be received into the mind?” Peter answered, “This, my friend Clement, can be acquired if someone becomes fully convinced that enemies who for a time maltreat those they hate become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors. The path to acquiring this, my friend Clement, is one particular path: the fear of God. For at first the person who fears God cannot love his neighbor as himself, since such a thing does not enter the soul by command. Yet through fear directed toward God he can do what those who love do. Then, once he has thus performed the deeds of love, loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom. And so, as she gives birth to humane thoughts, she makes the one who has acquired her immortal, as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay.” Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness, evening overtook us, and we turned to sleep.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"οὐκ οἴομαι δυνατὸν ἀνθρωπείᾳ προσεῖναι φύσει","chosen":"I do not think that the ability ... can belong to human nature","rationale":"προσεῖναι expresses being present in or belonging to something; δυνατός supplies the ability whose presence in human nature Clement doubts."},{"source_quote":"ἡ φιλανθρωπία πολλοῦ δίδοται","chosen":"humaneness ... is given at great cost","rationale":"πολλοῦ δίδοται presents humaneness as something obtained for much or at a high price, not as something easily granted."},{"source_quote":"Πῶς οὖν σύνεστιν ἐν νῷ λαβεῖν;","chosen":"How, then, can it be received into the mind?","rationale":"The rendering preserves both acquisition language in λαβεῖν and the explicitly mental location ἐν νῷ. The question may more idiomatically mean, “How, then, can one acquire it?”"},{"source_quote":"αἰωνίου κολάσεως ἀπαλλαγῆς αὐτοῖς αἴτιοι γίνονται· προσέτι δὲ αὐτοὺς ὡς εὐεργέτας σφόδρα ἀγαπήσουσιν","chosen":"become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors","rationale":"The sufferers are taken as the referents of αὐτοῖς and as the understood subject of ἀγαπήσουσιν, while αὐτούς refers back to the enemies. Repeating “those people” makes the selected referents clear without changing the claim."},{"source_quote":"ἐπεὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο κελεύσει οὐ προσέρχεται τῇ ψυχῇ","chosen":"since such a thing does not enter the soul by command","rationale":"κελεύσει is taken instrumentally: love does not arise in the soul merely through being commanded."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ὡς νύμφη οὖσα προσφέρεται ὡς νυμφίῳ τῷ φόβῳ","chosen":"loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom","rationale":"The personification and bridal image are preserved. τὸ ἀγαπᾶν is formally an infinitive, so “loving itself” retains the emphasis on the act or condition of loving."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς φιλανθρώπους τίκτουσα λογισμοὺς","chosen":"as she gives birth to humane thoughts","rationale":"The feminine pronoun follows the immediately preceding bride imagery, and τίκτουσα retains the explicit image of giving birth."},{"source_quote":"ὡς εἰκόνα θεοῦ ὁμοίαν, ὑπὸ φθορᾶς ὑβρισθῆναι μὴ δυναμένην τὴν αὐτοῦ φύσιν","chosen":"as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay","rationale":"ὁμοίαν is taken with the image as resembling God. ὑβρίζω is rendered “violation” to preserve its stronger force than simple damage, while φθορά is “decay” or “corruption.”"},{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον","chosen":"Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness","rationale":"Peter is taken as the omitted subject of the genitive participle ἐκθεμένου, with λόγον as its accusative object. The printed ὁμῶς is rendered “likewise”; a concessive “all the same” is another possible understanding."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον","issue":"The active genitive participle ἐκθεμένου has no explicitly stated genitive subject; Peter is readily supplied from the preceding speech, and λόγον functions as its object. The printed adverb ὁμῶς may mean “likewise” or “together,” while a sense such as “all the same” would normally be written ὅμως. The supplied reading remains translatable without emendation.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
